content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, Sheol is most commonly understood as the Old Testament's term for the realm or abode of the dead — the grave or underworld to which all the dead, righteous and wicked alike, descend. It symbolizes the shadowy, silent condition of death itself rather than a place of active punishment. Modern translations therefore typically render it 'the grave,' 'the pit,' 'the realm of the dead,' or transliterate it as 'Sheol,' while older versions (notably the KJV) often rendered it 'hell,' contributing to popular conflation with the place of final punishment. In Christian theology Sheol is usually treated as the intermediate state of the dead prior to resurrection, corresponding to Greek 'Hades' in the New Testament, and is distinguished from Gehenna (the place of final judgment).", "primary_basis": ["Genesis 37:35 (Jacob expects to go down to Sheol mourning — a righteous man descends there)", "Numbers 16:30-33 (Korah's company goes down alive into Sheol/the pit)", "1 Samuel 2:6 (the LORD brings down to Sheol and raises up)", "Job 14:13 (Job asks to be hidden in Sheol)", "Psalm 6:5 (in death there is no remembrance; in Sheol who gives thanks?)", "Psalm 16:10 (you will not abandon my soul to Sheol — quoted in Acts 2:27, 31 as Hades)", "Psalm 88:3-12 (descriptions of Sheol as the pit, darkness, the land of forgetfulness)", "Ecclesiastes 9:5, 10 (no work, knowledge, or wisdom in Sheol)", "Isaiah 14:9-11, 15 (Sheol stirred to meet the king of Babylon)", "Ezekiel 32:21-27 (the slain nations lying in Sheol)", "Jonah 2:2 (from the belly of Sheol I cried)", "Acts 2:27, 31 and Revelation 20:13-14 (Hades as the NT counterpart, ultimately emptied and destroyed)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Sheol simply means the literal grave or the state of nonexistence/unconsciousness in death, with no conscious survival of any kind — the position of conditionalists, annihilationists, Seventh-day Adventists, and Jehovah's Witnesses ('soul sleep'), who stress that the dead in Sheol know nothing.", "basis": ["Ecclesiastes 9:5, 10", "Psalm 6:5", "Psalm 115:17", "Psalm 146:4", "Job 14:10-12"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Sheol/Hades as a divided or two-compartment intermediate realm — a place of comfort for the righteous ('Abraham's bosom' or Paradise) and a place of conscious torment for the wicked, awaiting final judgment. Often connected with the doctrine of Christ's descent to the dead ('he descended into hell') and, in some traditions, the 'harrowing of hell' or limbus patrum.", "basis": ["Luke 16:19-31 (the rich man and Lazarus)", "Luke 23:43 (Paradise)", "1 Peter 3:18-20; 4:6 (Christ preaching to the spirits in prison)", "Ephesians 4:8-10 (he descended to the lower parts of the earth)", "Acts 2:27, 31"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Sheol as 'hell' in the popular sense — a place of fiery punishment for the wicked — following the KJV's frequent rendering of Sheol as 'hell.' This reading conflates Sheol with Gehenna and persists in some traditionalist and popular preaching, though most scholars and modern translations reject the equation.", "basis": ["KJV renderings of Psalm 9:17; Deuteronomy 32:22; Proverbs 15:24; Isaiah 5:14", "Popular association with Matthew 25:41, 46 and Revelation 20:14-15"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Sheol as primarily a poetic/metaphorical personification of death's power — an insatiable devourer or hostile force from which God delivers, rather than a spatial location; emphasized in some critical and literary scholarship on Hebrew poetry.", "basis": ["Proverbs 27:20; 30:15-16 (Sheol is never satisfied)", "Isaiah 5:14 (Sheol enlarges its appetite)", "Habakkuk 2:5", "Hosea 13:14 (O Sheol, where is your sting? — cited in 1 Corinthians 15:55)", "Psalm 18:4-5 (cords of Sheol entangled me)"], "prominence": "common"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is broad scholarly and mainstream ecclesial consensus that Sheol denotes the common realm/state of the dead (the grave or underworld) in the Hebrew Bible, not the place of final fiery punishment; this is reflected in virtually all modern translations and standard reference works. However, the theological freight assigned to it — conscious intermediate state versus unconscious 'sleep,' divided compartments versus undifferentiated shadow-existence — remains genuinely disputed among traditions (Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed, evangelical conditionalist, Adventist, Jehovah's Witnesses). The consensus concerns the core referent (the abode/state of the dead), not the anthropology of what the dead experience there. The KJV's rendering 'hell' is the main historical source of popular divergence from the scholarly consensus."}
